-- ============================================================================
-- solution.sql — R4 case: "Schema + Bulk Load + Optimize"
-- ============================================================================
-- One self-contained script, runnable top to bottom on a fresh database:
--
--     psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -f solution.sql
--
-- Contents
--   1. DDL       : the four tables exactly as specified in schema.sql.
--   2. BULK LOAD : ~100,000 orders + their order_items (~300,000 lines),
--                  fully set-based (one INSERT ... SELECT generate_series()
--                  per table — no row-by-row loops).
--   3. INDEX     : the index that serves target_query.sql.
--   4. STATS     : VACUUM (ANALYZE) so the planner has fresh statistics and
--                  the freshly loaded pages are marked all-visible.
--   5. SELF-CHECK: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) of target_query.sql.
--
-- Bulk-load plan (section 2)
-- --------------------------
-- Real-world bulk loads stage the raw data first and then fan it out into
-- the normalized tables with set-based INSERT ... SELECT (or COPY).  With no
-- external data file, the staging payload is generated deterministically in
-- SQL with a fixed seed:
--
--   * 20,000 customers, 5,000 products (10 categories).
--   * 100,000 orders:
--       - status      : COMPLETED ~50%, PENDING ~20%, CANCELLED ~15%,
--                       REFUNDED ~15%  (one uniform draw per order).
--       - order_date  : uniform over 2025-06-01 .. 2026-09-30 (487 days).
--       - total_amount: the sum of the order's line items (kept consistent).
--   * 1..5 order_items per order (~300,000 lines, avg 3.0), each referencing
--     an existing product with the catalog unit_price.
--
-- Optimization (section 3)
-- ------------------------
-- target_query.sql restricts orders by an equality on status and a range on
-- order_date, and only needs order_id from that table for the join.  A btree
-- on (status, order_date) matches both predicates (equality on the leading
-- column, range on the second), and INCLUDE (order_id) makes the index
-- covering, so the orders side of the join is an Index Only Scan that never
-- touches the heap.  With ~28% of orders matching (50% COMPLETED x ~56% of
-- the date span), a non-covering index would likely lose to a seq scan.
-- ============================================================================

-- ============================================================================
-- 1) DDL — four tables, exactly as specified in schema.sql
--    (no indexes here; the optimization index is added after the load)
-- ============================================================================

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS order_items CASCADE;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS orders CASCADE;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS products CASCADE;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS customers CASCADE;

CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id   bigint PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_name varchar(120) NOT NULL,
    email         varchar(200) NOT NULL,
    country       varchar(2)   NOT NULL,
    created_at    timestamptz  NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE products (
    product_id   bigint PRIMARY KEY,
    product_name varchar(160) NOT NULL,
    category     varchar(60)  NOT NULL,
    unit_price   numeric(10,2) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id     bigint PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id  bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(customer_id),
    order_date   timestamptz NOT NULL,
    status       varchar(20) NOT NULL,
    total_amount numeric(12,2) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE order_items (
    order_item_id bigint PRIMARY KEY,
    order_id      bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(order_id),
    product_id    bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES products(product_id),
    quantity      integer NOT NULL,
    unit_price    numeric(10,2) NOT NULL
);

-- ============================================================================
-- 2) BULK LOAD
-- ============================================================================

-- Fixed seed => the dataset (and therefore every timing/plan below) is
-- reproducible from run to run.

-- 2a) Customers: 20,000 ----------------------------------------------- ~20k rows

SELECT g.i,
       'Customer #' || lpad(g.i::text, 6, '0'),
       'customer' || g.i || '@example.com',
       (ARRAY['US','GB','DE','FR','JP','BR','IN','CA'])[1 + floor(random() * 8)::int],
       timestamptz '2023-01-01' + random() * interval '900 days'
FROM   generate_series(1, 20000) AS g(i);

-- 2b) Products: 5,000, 10 categories ---------------------------------- ~5k rows

INSERT INTO products (product_id, product_name, category, unit_price)
SELECT g.i,
       'Product #' || lpad(g.i::text, 5, '0'),
       (ARRAY['Electronics','Books','Home & Kitchen','Toys & Games','Sports',
              'Clothing','Grocery','Beauty & Health','Automotive','Garden'
             ])[1 + floor(random() * 10)::int],
       round((10 + random() * 990)::numeric, 2)
FROM   generate_series(1, 5000) AS g(i);

-- 2c) Stage the line items: 1..5 items per order --------------------- ~300k rows
--     Generated up front (in a temp table) so that orders.total_amount can
--     be loaded consistent with its items in a single set-based INSERT.

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS staged_order_items;

CREATE TEMP TABLE staged_order_items AS
SELECT it.order_id,
       it.product_id,
       it.quantity,
       p.unit_price
FROM   (
        SELECT o.order_id,
               (1 + floor(random() * 5000))::bigint AS product_id,  -- existing product
               (1 + floor(random() * 4))::int      AS quantity      -- 1..4 units
        FROM   (
                SELECT g.i AS order_id,

**`/work/solution.sql`** — one self-contained script (`psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -f solution.sql`, ~2s end-to-end) with five sections:

**1. DDL** — the four tables exactly as specified in `schema.sql` (PKs and FKs inline).

**2. Bulk load** — fully set-based, deterministic (`setseed`), staged like a real bulk load:
- 20,000 customers, 5,000 products (10 categories)
- **100,000 orders**: `status` drawn 50/20/15/15 (measured: COMPLETED **50.19%**, PENDING 19.66%, CANCELLED 15.09%, REFUNDED 15.07%); `order_date` uniform over exactly **2025-06-01..2026-09-30** (all 487 days present); `total_amount` = sum of its line items (0 inconsistencies)
- **300,057 order_items** (1–5 per order, avg 3.00), referencing existing products at catalog price; a temp staging table feeds both the `orders` totals and the `order_items` insert so the two stay consistent
- Verified: no orphaned FKs anywhere

**3. Index** — the key design decision:
```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status_order_date
    ON orders (status, order_date) INCLUDE (order_id);
```
I measured all three scenarios on the loaded dataset (28,063 of 100,000 orders match the filter ≈ 28% selectivity):

| Index on orders | Plan | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| none | **Seq Scan on orders** (the problem) | 2400 |
| plain `(status, order_date)` | Bitmap Heap Scan (wins, but thin margin — still touches ~every heap page) | ~1715 |
| `(status, order_date) INCLUDE (order_id)` | **Index Only Scan, Heap Fetches: 0** | ~1105 |

`(status, order_date)` maps both predicates (equality + range) to index conditions; `INCLUDE (order_id)` covers the only other column the query reads from `orders`, so the join's orders side never touches the heap — the fastest and most cache-independent plan.
